query.original_query: interpretability foundation model dose-response Hill equation saturation pharmacology mechanism representation

sub_queries.semantic_query: dose-response curves Hill equation saturation effects in interpretability analysis of foundation models internal representations and mechanistic understanding
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the application of dose-response modeling, specifically the Hill equation, to characterize saturation effects in the internal representations of foundation models during mechanistic interpretability analysis. Using sparse autoencoders applied to residual stream activations, we analyze how feature activation magnitudes scale with input intensity, revealing that many monosemantic features exhibit sigmoidal response curves consistent with cooperative binding dynamics. Our analysis demonstrates that the Hill coefficient varies across features, with some showing ultrasensitive transitions and others gradual saturation, mirroring dose-response relationships in biological systems. We find that saturation plateaus correspond to regions where reconstruction fidelity degrades, suggesting that feature absorption and dead features may arise from nonlinear activation thresholds. By fitting Hill curves to feature responses across layers of a vision-language model, we show that saturation onset correlates with the depth of the residual stream and the specificity of the encoded concept. Results indicate that mechanistic understanding of feature steering and polysemanticity benefits from modeling these nonlinear dynamics, as saturation effects limit the interpretability of high-magnitude activations and constrain the linearity assumptions underlying dictionary learning approaches.

sub_queries.semantic_query: dose-response curves Hill equation saturation pharmacokinetics pharmacodynamics receptor binding mechanism of action
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the relationship between receptor occupancy and functional response for a series of structurally related compounds at the target receptor. Using radioligand binding assays, we measured equilibrium dissociation constants (Kd) and constructed dose-response curves to determine half-maximal effective concentrations (EC50). The Hill coefficient was estimated for each compound to assess binding cooperativity. Pharmacokinetic parameters, including clearance and volume of distribution, were determined following intravenous administration in a rodent model. Results indicate that the observed pharmacodynamic effect is consistent with a saturable receptor binding mechanism, where the Hill equation accurately describes the relationship between plasma concentration and response. Findings support the hypothesis that the mechanism of action involves competitive antagonism at the orthosteric binding site, with a strong correlation between in vitro binding affinity and in vivo potency. These data provide a quantitative framework for predicting in vivo efficacy from in vitro receptor binding profiles.

papers.title: Investigating Saturation Effects in Integrated Gradients
papers.research_question: How do saturated regions along the integral path affect Integrated Gradients attributions, and can a variant focusing on unsaturated regions improve attribution quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes saturation effects in Integrated Gradients, finding that gradients in saturated regions disproportionately impact attributions, and proposes a variant (Split IG) that focuses on unsaturated regions, showing improved model faithfulness and lower sensitivity to noise.
papers.conclusion: Users of Integrated Gradients should be aware of saturation effects and consider comparing attributions from saturated and unsaturated regions, as Split IG can provide more faithful and less noisy explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Gradients in saturated regions (where model output changes minimally) contribute disproportionately to standard Integrated Gradients attributions.
The proposed Split IG variant, which restricts the integral to unsaturated regions, produces attributions with higher model faithfulness (measured by ABPC) and lower sensitivity to input perturbations compared to standard IG.
Attributions from saturated regions (RightIG) are noisier and less faithful to the model than those from unsaturated regions (LeftIG).
The choice of attributing to logits versus softmax outputs can affect the magnitude of gradients in saturated regions.
papers.limitation:
Quantitative evaluation of attribution methods is challenging due to the lack of ground truth for input importance.
Evaluation is primarily conducted on ImageNet classification networks; generality to other tasks and architectures requires further study.
future_direction: Examine the effect of baseline choices and model architecture on saturation.
Understand the impacts of saturation on other gradient-based attribution methods and variants of IG.
Evaluate whether removing saturated areas improves attributions beyond standard image classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Integrated Gradients has become a popular method for post-hoc model interpretability. De-spite its popularity, the composition and relative impact of different regions of the integral path are not well understood. We explore these effects and find that gradients in saturated regions of this path, where model output changes minimally, contribute disproportionately to the computed attribution. We propose a variant of IntegratedGradients which primarily captures gradients in unsaturated regions and evaluate this method on ImageNet classification networks. We find that this attribution technique shows higher model faithfulness and lower sensitivity to noise com-pared with standard Integrated Gradients. A note-book illustrating our computations and results is available at https://github.com/vivekmig/captum-1/tree/ExpandedIG.

papers.title: Scale Alone Does not Improve Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision Models
papers.research_question: Does scaling model and dataset size improve the mechanistic interpretability of vision models at the level of individual units?
papers.core_contribution: Scaling model and dataset size does not improve the mechanistic interpretability of vision models at the level of individual units, and latest-generation models may even be less interpretable than older ones.
papers.conclusion: Scale alone does not improve mechanistic interpretability in vision models; explicit design for interpretability is needed, and the released dataset can facilitate research on automated interpretability measures.
papers.key_findings:
No practically relevant differences in interpretability across nine vision models of varying scales, indicating that scaling does not improve interpretability.
Feature visualizations are less helpful than natural exemplars for explaining unit activations across all models, including adversarially robust models.
Interpretability does not increase with model classification performance or human-likeness, and may even decrease for feature visualizations as accuracy increases.
For models pre-trained on large datasets (Clip ResNet and Clip ViT), later layers are more interpretable, suggesting a shift in interpretability across layers.
Interpretability drops sharply when the task difficulty increases slightly, indicating that human understanding of unit behavior is limited.
papers.limitation:
The study only employed two widely-used explanation methods (feature visualizations and natural exemplars), which may not capture all aspects of interpretability.
Feature visualizations for ViT models were not evaluated due to methodological challenges, limiting the comparison for transformer architectures.
future_direction: Designing models explicitly for interpretability rather than relying on scale.
Developing automated interpretability measures using the released dataset to avoid costly human evaluations.
Further research on interpretability methods beyond feature visualizations and natural exemplars.
papers.abstract: In light of the recent widespread adoption of AI systems, understanding the internal information processing of neural networks has become increasingly critical. Most recently, machine vision has seen remarkable progress by scaling neural networks to unprecedented levels in dataset and model size. We here ask whether this extraordinary increase in scale also positively impacts the field of mechanistic interpretability. In other words, has our understanding of the inner workings of scaled neural networks improved as well? We use a psychophysical paradigm to quantify one form of mechanistic interpretability for a diverse suite of nine models and find no scaling effect for interpretability - neither for model nor dataset size. Specifically, none of the investigated state-of-the-art models are easier to interpret than the GoogLeNet model from almost a decade ago. Latest-generation vision models appear even less interpretable than older architectures, hinting at a regression rather than improvement, with modern models sacrificing interpretability for accuracy. These results highlight the need for models explicitly designed to be mechanistically interpretable and the need for more helpful interpretability methods to increase our understanding of networks at an atomic level. We release a dataset containing more than 130'000 human responses from our psychophysical evaluation of 767 units across nine models. This dataset facilitates research on automated instead of human-based interpretability evaluations, which can ultimately be leveraged to directly optimize the mechanistic interpretability of models.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: A Survey on Mechanistic Interpretability for Multi-Modal Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can LLM interpretability methods be adapted to multimodal foundation models, and what are the mechanistic differences between unimodal and multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability for multimodal foundation models, introducing a taxonomy and comparing insights between unimodal and multimodal models to highlight research gaps.
papers.conclusion: The survey reviews mechanistic understanding methods for MMFMs, introduces a taxonomy differentiating interpretability methods adapted from language models and those designed for multimodal models, and compares mechanistic insights to identify gaps and their impact on downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-based interpretability methods can be extended to MMFMs with moderate adjustments, particularly when treating visual and textual inputs similarly.
Novel multimodal challenges arise such as interpreting visual embeddings in human-understandable terms, necessitating new dedicated analysis methods.
While interpretability aids downstream tasks, applications like hallucination mitigation and model editing remain underdeveloped in multimodal models compared to language models.
There is a substantial gap between the interpretability of LLMs and MMFMs, with a lack of unified benchmarks and tools for multimodal interpretability.
The survey proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy for mechanistic interpretability in multimodal models based on model family, interpretability techniques, and applications.
papers.limitation:
The survey mainly focuses on image-text multimodal models without considering other modalities such as video, time series, or 3D.
The survey does not contain experimental analysis because of the lack of unified benchmarks.
The survey only focuses on transformer-based or diffusion models, without considering novel model architectures such as MAMBA.
future_direction: Extending mechanistic interpretability techniques to analyze unified vision-text understanding and generation models.
Developing sequential batch model editing techniques for multimodal models, including diffusion and multimodal language models.
Exploring the effectiveness of sparse autoencoders and their variants for controlling and steering multimodal models.
papers.abstract: The rise of foundation models has transformed machine learning research, prompting efforts to uncover their inner workings and develop more efficient and reliable applications for better control. While significant progress has been made in interpreting Large Language Models (LLMs), multimodal foundation models (MMFMs) - such as contrastive vision-language models, generative vision-language models, and text-to-image models - pose unique interpretability challenges beyond unimodal frameworks. Despite initial studies, a substantial gap remains between the interpretability of LLMs and MMFMs. This survey explores two key aspects: (1) the adaptation of LLM interpretability methods to multimodal models and (2) understanding the mechanistic differences between unimodal language models and crossmodal systems. By systematically reviewing current MMFM analysis techniques, we propose a structured taxonomy of interpretability methods, compare insights across unimodal and multimodal architectures, and highlight critical research gaps.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
papers.research_question: How can we unify existing methods for interpreting model predictions and assign feature importance values that satisfy desirable properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SHAP, a unified framework for interpreting model predictions that unifies six existing methods and provides a unique solution with desirable properties, leading to new methods with improved computational performance and consistency with human intuition.
papers.conclusion: The SHAP framework identifies the class of additive feature importance methods and shows there is a unique solution in this class that adheres to desirable properties, providing a unified approach to model interpretation with improved estimation methods.
papers.key_findings:
SHAP unifies six existing feature attribution methods: LIME, DeepLIFT, Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation, Shapley regression values, Shapley sampling values, and Quantitative Input Influence.
SHAP values are the unique solution in the class of additive feature attribution methods that satisfy local accuracy, missingness, and consistency.
Kernel SHAP provides more accurate estimates with fewer model evaluations than previous sampling-based methods like Shapley sampling values.
SHAP values are more consistent with human intuition than LIME and DeepLIFT in user studies on simple models.
Deep SHAP, a compositional approximation for deep networks, improves upon DeepLIFT by better approximating Shapley values.
papers.limitation: Exact computation of SHAP values is challenging and requires approximations, which may rely on assumptions like feature independence or model linearity.
future_direction: Developing faster model-type-specific estimation methods that make fewer assumptions.
Integrating work on estimating interaction effects from game theory.
Defining new explanation model classes.
papers.abstract: Understanding why a model makes a certain prediction can be as crucial as the prediction's accuracy in many applications. However, the highest accuracy for large modern datasets is often achieved by complex models that even experts struggle to interpret, such as ensemble or deep learning models, creating a tension between accuracy and interpretability. In response, various methods have recently been proposed to help users interpret the predictions of complex models, but it is often unclear how these methods are related and when one method is preferable over another. To address this problem, we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its novel components include: (1) the identification of a new class of additive feature importance measures, and (2) theoretical results showing there is a unique solution in this class with a set of desirable properties. The new class unifies six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties. Based on insights from this unification, we present new methods that show improved computational performance and/or better consistency with human intuition than previous approaches.

papers.title: An unexpected unity among methods for interpreting model predictions
papers.research_question: How can we interpret model predictions by estimating the importance of input features, and how does a model-agnostic additive representation based on Shapley values unify current methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a model-agnostic additive representation of feature importance based on Shapley values (ES values) unifies several existing interpretability methods (LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, Shapley regression values) and is the only solution satisfying key axioms of efficiency, symmetry, and monotonicity.
papers.conclusion: ES values provide a unified, axiomatically justified framework for interpreting model predictions, which can be used to improve existing methods and create novel visual explanations.
papers.key_findings:
ES values unify LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, and Shapley regression values under a single framework.
ES values are the only additive feature attribution method that satisfies the axioms of efficiency, symmetry, and monotonicity, providing an optimal solution.
The Shapley kernel derived from these axioms leads to more accurate and efficient estimation of feature importance compared to heuristically chosen kernels.
ES values provide theoretical justification for specific parameter choices in existing methods, such as the kernel for LIME and linearization for DeepLIFT.
ES values can be visualized to explain individual predictions and reveal patterns of model behavior across a dataset.
papers.abstract: Understanding why a model made a certain prediction is crucial in many data science fields. Interpretable predictions engender appropriate trust and provide insight into how the model may be improved. However, with large modern datasets the best accuracy is often achieved by complex models even experts struggle to interpret, which creates a tension between accuracy and interpretability. Recently, several methods have been proposed for interpreting predictions from complex models by estimating the importance of input features. Here, we present how a model-agnostic additive representation of the importance of input features unifies current methods. This representation is optimal, in the sense that it is the only set of additive values that satisfies important properties. We show how we can leverage these properties to create novel visual explanations of model predictions. The thread of unity that this representation weaves through the literature indicates that there are common principles to be learned about the interpretation of model predictions that apply in many scenarios.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: How 'Neural' is a Neural Foundation Model?
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are their representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The recurrent module of the neural foundation model shows brain-like representational properties, while the feedforward encoder and readout module have limitations; design changes are suggested for better biological alignment.
papers.conclusion: The FNN is only a partial digital twin of the mouse visual system; its recurrent module is most brain-like, but design improvements in early recurrence and readout constraints could enhance biological alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The recurrent module achieves the highest stimulus separability and closest alignment with biological visual cortex.
The feedforward encoder lacks biologically plausible temporal patterns and contains non-selective neurons.
The readout module uses numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
Decoding trajectories in the recurrent stage show tubular structure but fewer crossings than biological data, indicating less complex dynamics.
Encoding manifolds reveal that the FNN's neuronal organization, especially in the readout, is clustered by feature maps and differs from the continuous topology of biological cortex.
papers.limitation:
The FNN does not fully capture the complexity of neural dynamics, as evidenced by fewer crossings in decoding trajectories compared to biological data.
The readout module's highly clustered, feature-map-based organization is not brain-like.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence in early encoder stages.
Constraining features in the readout module to be more biologically plausible.
Investigate more complex temporal processing to better match biological dynamics.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns. Our 'tubularity' metric quantifies this stimulus-dependent development of neural activity as biologically plausible. The readout module achieves high fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, this study provides a window into the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns. Our findings suggest design changes that could bring neural foundation models into closer alignment with biological systems: introducing recurrence in early encoder stages, and constraining features in the readout module.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
