REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: Decompose the model: Mechanistic interpretability in image models with Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG)
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be achieved in image models by systematically tracing the pathway from input to output across an entire dataset, moving beyond class-specific explanations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel approach for mechanistic interpretability in image models, using Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors, and a new Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method to trace their causal contributions across layers for a dataset-wide analysis.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach for extracting and attributing concepts within image models, enabling a comprehensive layer-wise analysis that advances mechanistic interpretability by moving from class-specific to dataset-wide explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract and attribute 'shared concepts' that are common across similar classes, unlike class-specific explanation methods.
The proposed concept extraction method using bisecting k-means clustering outperforms other methods (like Sparse AutoEncoder and dictionary learning) in fidelity metrics (C-Deletion and C-Insertion) across most layers.
The Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method effectively quantifies the causal relationships between concept vectors across different layers, validated by inter-layer deletion/insertion experiments.
The approach provides a holistic, dataset-wide understanding of model behavior, tracing how concepts are constructed and aggregated from lower to higher layers.
future_direction: Extending the method to other deep learning architectures, such as Transformer models.
More thoroughly investigating the implications of analyzing entire datasets rather than focusing solely on class-specific explanations.
papers.abstract: In the field of eXplainable AI (XAI) in language models, the progression from local explanations of individual decisions to global explanations with high-level concepts has laid the groundwork for mechanistic interpretability, which aims to decode the exact operations. However, this paradigm has not been adequately explored in image models, where existing methods have primarily focused on class-specific interpretations. This paper introduces a novel approach to systematically trace the entire pathway from input through all intermediate layers to the final output within the whole dataset. We utilize Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors. Then, we calculate the relevance between concept vectors with our Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG), enabling a comprehensive, dataset-wide analysis of model behavior. We validate our method of concept extraction and concept attribution in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Our approach advances the understanding of semantic significance within image models, offering a holistic view of their operational mechanics.

papers.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
papers.research_question: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? The paper proposes a benchmark to provide a basis for comparisons.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MIB, a benchmark for mechanistic interpretability with two tracks (circuit localization and causal variable localization) to enable meaningful comparisons of interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: MIB provides a standardized benchmark for comparing mechanistic interpretability methods, enabling meaningful evaluations and demonstrating progress in the field.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization.
Supervised Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) performs best on causal variable localization.
Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are not better than non-featurized hidden vectors (neurons) for causal variable localization.
MIB enables meaningful comparisons and shows real progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The set of models and tasks is incomplete, limiting generalizability.
The metrics may not capture all aspects of interpretability that researchers care about.
The benchmark focuses on localization and featurization, leaving out other mechanistic interpretability goals like editing or control.
future_direction: Expand MIB to include more models and tasks.
Develop more comprehensive metrics that capture other aspects of interpretability.
Extend the benchmark to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? In pursuit of lasting evaluation standards, we propose MIB, a Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, with two tracks spanning four tasks and five models. MIB favors methods that precisely and concisely recover relevant causal pathways or causal variables in neural language models. The circuit localization track compares methods that locate the model components - and connections between them - most important for performing a task (e.g., attribution patching or information flow routes). The causal variable localization track compares methods that featurize a hidden vector, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs) or distributed alignment search (DAS), and align those features to a task-relevant causal variable. Using MIB, we find that attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization. For causal variable localization, we find that the supervised DAS method performs best, while SAE features are not better than neurons, i.e., non-featurized hidden vectors. These findings illustrate that MIB enables meaningful comparisons, and increases our confidence that there has been real progress in the field.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: A Theoretical Survey on Foundation Models
papers.core_contribution: This survey reviews interpretable methods grounded in machine learning theory (generalization analysis, expressive power analysis, dynamic behavior analysis) to interpret the inference capabilities, training dynamics, and ethical implications of foundation models.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes that interpretable methods based on machine learning theory provide a systematic way to understand foundation models, and suggests future research directions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner mechanisms of black-box foundation models (FMs) is essential yet challenging in artificial intelligence and its applications. Over the last decade, the long-running focus has been on their explainability, leading to the development of post-hoc explainable methods to rationalize the specific decisions already made by black-box FMs. However, these explainable methods have certain limitations in terms of faithfulness and resource requirement. Consequently, a new class of interpretable methods should be considered to unveil the underlying mechanisms of FMs in an accurate, comprehensive, heuristic, and resource-light way. This survey aims to review those interpretable methods that comply with the aforementioned principles and have been successfully applied to FMs. These methods are deeply rooted in machine learning theory, covering the analysis of generalization performance, expressive capability, and dynamic behavior. They provide a thorough interpretation of the entire workflow of FMs, ranging from the inference capability and training dynamics to their ethical implications. Ultimately, drawing upon these interpretations, this review identifies the next frontier research directions for FMs.

papers.title: Shape or Texture: Understanding Discriminative Features in CNNs
papers.research_question: What type of shape information is discriminative in CNNs, where is shape information encoded, and when does the network learn about object shape during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNNs learn shape information early in training, encode it primarily in the last few layers, and that shape encoding does not guarantee per-pixel semantic understanding.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a systematic study of shape encoding in CNNs, revealing important mechanisms that characterize a network's ability to encode shape information, which can inform the design of more robust and trustworthy computer vision algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs learn the majority of shape information during the first few epochs of training.
Shape information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN.
Biasing a CNN towards shape changes the number of shape encoding neurons in the last feature encoding stage.
Early layers also encode shape information, which can be combined with deeper layers for better shape extraction.
Encoding shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information.
papers.abstract: Contrasting the previous evidence that neurons in the later layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) respond to complex object shapes, recent studies have shown that CNNs actually exhibit a `texture bias': given an image with both texture and shape cues (e.g., a stylized image), a CNN is biased towards predicting the category corresponding to the texture. However, these previous studies conduct experiments on the final classification output of the network, and fail to robustly evaluate the bias contained (i) in the latent representations, and (ii) on a per-pixel level. In this paper, we design a series of experiments that overcome these issues. We do this with the goal of better understanding what type of shape information contained in the network is discriminative, where shape information is encoded, as well as when the network learns about object shape during training. We show that a network learns the majority of overall shape information at the first few epochs of training and that this information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN. Finally, we show that the encoding of shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information. The experimental results and findings provide a more accurate understanding of the behaviour of current CNNs, thus helping to inform future design choices.

papers.title: Incorporating Residual and Normalization Layers into Analysis of Masked Language Models
papers.research_question: How do residual connections and layer normalization affect the context-mixing in Transformer attention blocks compared to attention alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends norm-based analysis to include residual and layer normalization layers in Transformer attention blocks, showing that the context-mixing ratio is much lower than previously estimated, indicating that residual connections and layer normalization dominate the information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual connections and layer normalization significantly reduce the context-mixing effect of attention, leading to a much lower mixing ratio than previously assumed, which explains why discarding learned attention patterns often does not harm performance.
papers.key_findings:
The context-mixing ratio in attention blocks is much lower (16-19% on average) when considering residual and normalization layers compared to attention-only analysis (84-97%).
The preserving effect via residual connection is dominant over the mixing effect of attention.
The multi-head attention shrinks input vectors, and layer normalization further reduces the mixing ratio.
For masked tokens, the mixing ratio is higher in middle and later layers.
Larger BERT models show a negative correlation between word frequency and mixing ratio, indicating discounting of high-frequency words.
papers.limitation: Experiments limited to Transformer-based masked language models; feed-forward and embedding layers not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other Transformer variants
Extend analysis to feed-forward and embedding layers
papers.abstract: Transformer architecture has become ubiquitous in the natural language processing field. To interpret the Transformer-based models, their attention patterns have been extensively analyzed. However, the Transformer architecture is not only composed of the multihead attention; other components can also contribute to Transformers' progressive performance. In this study, we extended the scope of the analysis of Transformers from solely the attention patterns to the whole attention block, i.e., multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization. Our analysis of Transformer-based masked language models shows that the token-to-token interaction performed via attention has less impact on the intermediate representations than previously assumed. These results provide new intuitive explanations of existing reports; for example, discarding the learned attention patterns tends not to adversely affect the performance. The codes of our experiments are publicly available.

papers.title: Attention Saturation and Gradient Suppression at Inflection Layers: Diagnosing and Mitigating Bottlenecks in Transformer Adaptation
papers.research_question: How does output saturation cause gradient suppression at inflection layers during transformer fine-tuning, and how can this be diagnosed and mitigated to improve adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: We formalize the 'output saturation ⇒ gradient suppression' chain via standard cross-entropy+softmax derivations, revealing a fundamental mechanism: gradient suppression at inflection layers confines adaptation to high-level composition of existing features, preventing low-level reconstruction. We propose a suite of layer-wise diagnostic metrics and a diagnose-first, inject-light parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy: selectively injecting LoRA adapters at inflection layers to restore suppressed backward signals with minimal parameter overhead.
papers.conclusion: We ground the intuition of 'output saturation ⇒ gradient suppression' in layer-wise observable metrics, revealing that gradient suppression at inflection layers confines models to high-level composition. We propose selective LoRA injection based on inflection layers to restore suppressed backward pathways, demonstrating effectiveness in OVER models but limitations in UNDER models.
papers.key_findings:
OVER initialization benefits from inflection-layer LoRA injection while UNDER shows degradation.
Selective LoRA achieves higher accuracy with fewer parameters compared to uniform LoRA or full unfreezing.
Gradient suppression at inflection layers forces models to adapt via high-level composition rather than low-level reconstruction.
When base features are strong (OVER), unblocking inflection layers enables high-level composition; when weak (UNDER), low-level reconstruction requires full pathway unblocking.
Attention entropy and gradient norms consistently identify inflection layers across different settings.
papers.limitation:
Attention entropy is a correlational proxy for saturation, not a causal mechanism.
Results hold under BERT-base on English sentiment/review transfer—cross-lingual, cross-domain (e.g., NER, QA), and larger-scale models require separate validation.
SKI is heuristic with greedy implementation; learnable weighting may improve robustness.
Lack of PEFT baselines: Beyond LoRA Everywhere, comparisons with other PEFT methods would strengthen claims.
future_direction: Two-stage 'debiasing–relearning': introduce a short debiasing phase before fine-tuning.
Zero/near-zero-parameter plasticity injection: e.g., head dropout/re-initialization, attention temperature annealing.
Extension to other modalities and architectures: apply to vision Transformers, multimodal models, etc.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained Transformers often exhibit over-confidence in source patterns and difficulty in forming new target-domain patterns during fine-tuning. We formalize the mechanism of output saturation leading to gradient suppression through standard cross-entropy and softmax analysis, showing that gradient suppression at inflection layers confines adaptation to high-level recombination of existing features while preventing low-level reconstruction. We introduce a set of layer-wise diagnostic metrics -- attention entropy (saturation proxy), activation gradient norm, parameter gradient norm, and Delta-CKA under a shared PCA basis -- to identify inflection layers characterized by both low attention entropy and steep gradient decay. Building on these findings, we propose a diagnose-first, inject-light fine-tuning strategy: selectively inserting LoRA adapters at inflection layers to restore suppressed backward signals with minimal parameter overhead. Experiments on BERT-base transfer from SST-2 to Rotten Tomatoes under under-trained and over-trained source regimes reveal that over-trained initialization benefits from inflection-layer LoRA injection, while under-trained initialization suffers performance degradation. When base features are strong, unblocking inflection layers facilitates high-level compositional adaptation; when base features are weak, full-pathway unblocking is required for low-level reconstruction, as supported by joint analysis of layer-wise activation gradients and Delta-CKA dynamics.

papers.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Neurons with a Null-Calibrated Polysemanticity Index and Causal Patch Interventions
papers.research_question: How can one systematically identify and quantify polysemantic neurons in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Polysemanticity Index (PSI), a null-calibrated metric that combines geometric, categorical, and open-vocabulary semantic evidence to quantify when a neuron's top activations decompose into distinct, nameable concepts.
papers.conclusion: PSI provides a principled and practical tool for discovering, quantifying, and studying polysemantic units in neural networks, and can be extended to benchmark across architectures and training regimes or to study interpretability-performance trade-offs.
papers.key_findings:
PSI robustly distinguishes real neuronal structure from chance, achieving an AUROC of approximately 0.99 when separating late-layer neurons from a null baseline.
Polysemanticity is an emergent property of network depth, with neurons in later layers (layer4) exhibiting significantly higher PSI scores than those in earlier layers (layer3).
Causal patch-swap interventions validate that the feature prototypes discovered by PSI are causally relevant to the neuron's function, with aligned patches increasing activation significantly more than various controls.
PSI rankings are robust to reasonable variations in hyperparameters, such as the number of top patches K, and the optimal number of clusters for decomposable neurons is typically 2 or 3.
The semantic distinctness score (D) is sensitive to the choice of text encoder, indicating that 'semantic distinctness' is relative to the conceptual ontology of the language model used.
papers.limitation:
The open-vocabulary distinctness score (D) is dependent on the chosen multimodal model (CLIP) and its conceptual vocabulary, making semantic distinctness relative to the model's 'conceptual lens'.
The methodology relies on specific choices such as top-K mining (which may miss polysemanticity at moderate activation levels) and K-means clustering (which assumes convex clusters and may not capture complex topological structures).
future_direction: Benchmarking PSI across different architectures and training regimes.
Using PSI as a regularizer to study the trade-off between interpretability and performance.
Extending the PSI approach to analyze neurons or attention heads in large language models (LLMs) or transformers.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often contain polysemantic neurons that respond to multiple, sometimes unrelated, features, complicating mechanistic interpretability. We introduce the Polysemanticity Index (PSI), a null-calibrated metric that quantifies when a neuron's top activations decompose into semantically distinct clusters. PSI multiplies three independently calibrated components: geometric cluster quality (S), alignment to labeled categories (Q), and open-vocabulary semantic distinctness via CLIP (D). On a pretrained ResNet-50 evaluated with Tiny-ImageNet images, PSI identifies neurons whose activation sets split into coherent, nameable prototypes, and reveals strong depth trends: later layers exhibit substantially higher PSI than earlier layers. We validate our approach with robustness checks (varying hyperparameters, random seeds, and cross-encoder text heads), breadth analyses (comparing class-only vs. open-vocabulary concepts), and causal patch-swap interventions. In particular, aligned patch replacements increase target-neuron activation significantly more than non-aligned, random, shuffled-position, or ablate-elsewhere controls. PSI thus offers a principled and practical lever for discovering, quantifying, and studying polysemantic units in neural networks.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Network Models for Toxicity Prediction by Extracting Learned Chemical Features
papers.research_question: How can neural network models for toxicity prediction be interpreted by extracting learned chemical features from hidden layers?
papers.core_contribution: A novel method to interpret neural network predictions for toxicity by extracting chemical substructures from hidden neurons, validated on mutagenicity data and shown to be competitive with established attribution methods.
papers.conclusion: The study presents a novel method to extract learned chemical information from hidden layers of neural networks and use these to explain model predictions, complementing more established techniques for understanding neural network models for toxicity prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The activation of hidden neurons in a neural network trained for toxicity prediction can be linked to specific chemical substructures (toxicophores).
The proposed method can extract substructures that correspond to known toxicophores for mutagenicity.
The explanations provided by the method (IG_hidden) are competitive with and complementary to those from input feature attribution (IG_input).
The method works well for single-layer networks but for deeper layers, neurons tend to aggregate multiple features and become less specific.
papers.limitation:
One neuron may be activated by a range of diverse chemical substructures, making it impossible to assign a single cause to the activation of a particular neuron.
Relevant chemical features may activate a large number of different neurons across the network, making interpretation complex.
It could be that none of the identified substructures associated with a highly activated neuron match the test compound.
future_direction: Extending the approach to regression models.
Using more generic representations of substructures such as SMARTS.
Applying the method to other toxicity endpoints and datasets.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have become a popular machine-learning technique for the toxicity prediction of chemicals. However, due to their complex structure, it is difficult to understand predictions made by these models which limits confidence. Current techniques to tackle this problem such as SHAP or integrated gradients provide insights by attributing importance to the input features of individual compounds. While these methods have produced promising results in some cases, they do not shed light on how representations of compounds are transformed in hidden layers, which constitute how neural networks learn. We present a novel technique to interpret neural networks which identifies chemical substructures in training data found to be responsible for the activation of hidden neurons. For individual test compounds, the importance of hidden neurons is determined, and the associated substructures are leveraged to explain the model prediction. Using structural alerts for mutagenicity from the Derek Nexus expert system as ground truth, we demonstrate the validity of the approach and show that model explanations are competitive with and complementary to explanations obtained from an established feature attribution method.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Pathologies of Neural Models Make Interpretations Difficult
papers.research_question: Why do existing feature attribution interpretation methods for neural models fail, and how can the pathological behaviors they expose (e.g., overconfidence on nonsensical inputs) be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces input reduction, a method that exposes pathological behaviors in neural models (overconfidence on nonsensical, reduced inputs) and shows that fine-tuning with entropy regularization on these reduced examples mitigates the pathologies without harming accuracy on regular examples.
papers.conclusion: Input reduction reveals fundamental difficulties in interpreting neural models due to overconfidence and sensitivity, and suggests that improving uncertainty estimation and moving beyond bag-of-word heatmaps are important future directions for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Input reduction can iteratively remove 'unimportant' words from an input, often reducing it to one or two nonsensical words, without changing the model's prediction or significantly lowering its confidence.
Neural models are overconfident on these reduced 'rubbish' examples, which humans cannot answer correctly, revealing a failure of uncertainty estimation.
Gradient-based interpretation methods exhibit second-order sensitivity, where small input changes cause large shifts in the interpretation heatmap, even when the prediction remains stable.
Fine-tuning models with entropy regularization on reduced examples increases the length and human-interpretability of the reduced inputs without sacrificing accuracy on regular examples.
The pathologies are not due to overfitting alone, as they appear early in training, and are a fundamental issue with maximum likelihood training objectives.
future_direction: more thorough evaluation of interpretation methods
better uncertainty and confidence estimates
interpretation beyond bag-of-word heatmap
papers.abstract: One way to interpret neural model predictions is to highlight the most important input features-for example, a heatmap visualization over the words in an input sentence. In existing interpretation methods for NLP, a word's importance is determined by either input perturbation-measuring the decrease in model confidence when that word is removed-or by the gradient with respect to that word. To understand the limitations of these methods, we use input reduction, which iteratively removes the least important word from the input. This exposes pathological behaviors of neural models: the remaining words appear nonsensical to humans and are not the ones determined as important by interpretation methods. As we confirm with human experiments, the reduced examples lack information to support the prediction of any label, but models still make the same predictions with high confidence. To explain these counterintuitive results, we draw connections to adversarial examples and confidence calibration: pathological behaviors reveal difficulties in interpreting neural models trained with maximum likelihood. To mitigate their deficiencies, we fine-tune the models by encouraging high entropy outputs on reduced examples. Fine-tuned models become more interpretable under input reduction without accuracy loss on regular examples.

papers.title: Gradients of Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: How can we better quantify feature importance in deep neural networks when gradients at the input are small due to saturation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces interior gradients and integrated gradients, a method for feature attribution that addresses gradient saturation by examining gradients along a path from a baseline to the input, providing attributions that sum to the prediction score.
papers.conclusion: Interior gradients provide a method for quantifying feature importance in deep networks without instrumenting the network, making it easy to implement and apply for debugging and understanding model predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradients at the input can be tiny even for important features due to saturation in deep networks.
Interior gradients (gradients of counterfactual inputs along a scaling path) better capture feature importance than gradients at the original input.
Integrated gradients, obtained by cumulating interior gradients, have the attribution property that the importance scores sum to the prediction score and are invariant to network implementation.
The method is easy to implement and applicable to a variety of deep networks (image, molecular, language).
Integrated gradients outperform standard gradients in pixel ablation and localization evaluations on ImageNet.
papers.limitation:
Inability to capture feature interactions
Feature correlations can make attributions less interpretable
future_direction: Using interior gradients within training as a measure against saturation
Aggregating attributions across molecules to identify common features
papers.abstract: Gradients have been used to quantify feature importance in machine learning models. Unfortunately, in nonlinear deep networks, not only individual neurons but also the whole network can saturate, and as a result an important input feature can have a tiny gradient. We study various networks, and observe that this phenomena is indeed widespread, across many inputs. We propose to examine interior gradients, which are gradients of counterfactual inputs constructed by scaling down the original input. We apply our method to the GoogleNet architecture for object recognition in images, as well as a ligand-based virtual screening network with categorical features and an LSTM based language model for the Penn Treebank dataset. We visualize how interior gradients better capture feature importance. Furthermore, interior gradients are applicable to a wide variety of deep networks, and have the attribution property that the feature importance scores sum to the the prediction score. Best of all, interior gradients can be computed just as easily as gradients. In contrast, previous methods are complex to implement, which hinders practical adoption.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
papers.research_question: How can safety risks of large language models be uncovered by interpreting their safety mechanisms and generating effective attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Safety Concept Activation Vector framework to interpret LLM safety mechanisms and develops an SCAV-guided attack method that generates effective attacks with automatic hyperparameter selection, improving attack success rates and response quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers severe safety risks in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms using the SCAV framework.
papers.key_findings:
SCAV significantly improves attack success rates and response quality compared to baselines.
Generated attacks are transferable to black-box models like GPT-4 and other white-box LLMs.
Aligned LLMs show high vulnerability with average attack success rates up to 99.14%.
Existing unlearn methods may not fully erase harmful knowledge, as attacks still succeed.
Linear separability of embeddings indicates the formation of safety mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending SCAV to multimodal models
Developing more robust defense methods against attacks
papers.abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Interpretation of Deep CNN Based on Learning Feature Reconstruction With Feedback Weights
papers.research_question: How can we interpret a deep CNN by learning feature reconstruction with feedback weights to understand which features contribute to recognition and evaluate recognition success?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes attaching a feedback CNN to a pretrained feedforward CNN to interpret the deep CNN by reconstructing features and analyzing clusters in feature spaces, enabling accurate recovery of ground truth, generation of novel inputs, and identification of recognition errors.
papers.conclusion: The feedback weights provide a means to interpret the deep CNN, and the clustering-based interpretation and feature interpolation algorithm offer meaningful insights into neuron collaboration and recognition.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed approach accurately recovers ground truth input under data corruption.
It generates novel input data corresponding to an untrained feature vector without input data iterations.
It identifies incorrectly recognized input data by pinpointing the source of error in feature spaces.
The experiments on ModelNet datasets show higher accuracy than conventional approaches.
future_direction: Extend interpretation to connect semantic knowledge while extracting meaningful features using a deep neural network.
papers.abstract: Interpreting a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) involves identifying the features in a hierarchy of layers that contribute to recognition. Although the current approaches serve as methods to interpret a deep CNN, further advancement is required for a more accurate and efficient way of understanding how a hierarchy of features formed by a deep CNN contributes to recognition. In this paper, we propose attaching a feedback CNN to a pretrained feedforward CNN as a means of learning how recognition is performed by the feedforward CNN. In other words, the features reconstructed in a hierarchy of the feedback CNN represent those learned by the feedforward CNN. By analyzing how clusters are formed in the layers of feature spaces in the feedback CNN, we can interpret which features critically contribute to recognition. It also helps to evaluate whether or not recognition is done successfully. In order to show this, we experimentally verify the capabilities of the proposed approach in terms of 1) accurately recovering the ground truth input under data corruption; 2) generating novel input data corresponding to an untrained feature vector without input data iterations; and 3) identifying incorrectly recognized input data by pinpointing the source of the error in feature spaces. The experiments conducted on the ModelNet datasets indicate that the proposed approach offers an extended capability of interpreting a deep CNN as described above with higher accuracy than the conventional approaches.

papers.title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the dual problem to interpretability? The paper introduces patterning as the dual: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data leads to it.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces patterning as the dual of interpretability, using susceptibilities to derive data interventions that steer internal structure formation in neural networks, demonstrated in small language models and a synthetic task.
papers.conclusion: Patterning provides a principled approach to steering generalization by inverting the susceptibility relationship, with potential applications to AI alignment and control of internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting training data along the second principal susceptibility direction can accelerate or delay the formation of the induction circuit.
In the parentheses balancing task, patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution.
Susceptibility-guided interventions produce predictable changes in internal structures.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use small models (3M parameters) and simple tasks.
Susceptibility estimation is computationally expensive.
Focus on one-off interventions made at the start of training, not online control.
Theoretical framework assumes infinitesimal perturbations, while practical interventions are finite; understanding when the linear approximation breaks down is important.
Connection between observables and downstream behavior (e.g., safety properties) requires further study.
future_direction: Develop online control (adjusting data distribution dynamically during training).
Scale to larger models and more efficient methods.
Study the connection to safety properties and AI alignment applications.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how neural networks generalize beyond their training data by reverse-engineering their internal structures. We introduce patterning as the dual problem: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data produces it. Our approach is based on susceptibilities, which measure how posterior expectation values of observables respond to infinitesimal shifts in the data distribution. Inverting this linear response relationship yields the data intervention that steers the model toward a target internal configuration. We demonstrate patterning in a small language model, showing that re-weighting training data along principal susceptibility directions can accelerate or delay the formation of structure, such as the induction circuit. In a synthetic parentheses balancing task where multiple algorithms achieve perfect training accuracy, we show that patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution. These results establish that the same mathematical framework used to read internal structure can be inverted to write it.

papers.title: Probing for Predicate Argument Structures in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: Do pretrained language models (PLMs) encode the argument structure of a predicate in its contextual representation? How are predicate senses and their argument structures encoded across layers, and how do they differ between verbal and nominal predicates and across languages?
papers.core_contribution: PLMs encode predicate argument structures in their contextual representations, with senses and rolesets encoded at different layers, and verbal and nominal predicates are represented differently. Integrating this knowledge improves SRL performance.
papers.conclusion: Probing PLMs for predicate argument structures reveals how they encode semantic information and provides insights that can be used to improve SRL systems.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode predicate argument structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate.
Predicate senses and their argument structures are encoded at different layers in PLMs.
Verbal and nominal predicate argument structures are represented differently across the layers of a PLM, making transfer between them non-trivial.
Multilingual PLMs encode predicate argument structure information similarly across English and Chinese.
Integrating predicate-argument structure knowledge into an SRL model via weighted averaging of layers and multi-task learning improves performance.
future_direction: cross-lingual transfer learning for SRL
using all layers of PLMs for SRL
papers.abstract: Thanks to the effectiveness and wide availability of modern pretrained language models (PLMs), recently proposed approaches have achieved remarkable results in dependencyand span-based, multilingual and cross-lingual Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). These results have prompted researchers to investigate the inner workings of modern PLMs with the aim of understanding how, where, and to what extent they encode information about SRL. In this paper, we follow this line of research and probe for predicate argument structures in PLMs. Our study shows that PLMs do encode semantic structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate, and also provides insights into the correlation between predicate senses and their structures, the degree of transferability between nominal and verbal structures, and how such structures are encoded across languages. Finally, we look at the practical implications of such insights and demonstrate the benefits of embedding predicate argument structure information into an SRL model.

papers.title: A Categorisation of Post-hoc Explanations for Predictive Models
papers.research_question: How can post-hoc explanations for predictive models be categorized to aid model interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Extends and tests a hierarchical categorization of post-hoc explanation techniques for interpretability of predictive models.
papers.conclusion: The article provides an overview of interpretability aspects, proposes a categorization, and highlights areas for future research such as bug-free models and axiomatic treatments.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a hierarchical view of interpretability with transparency and post-hoc explanations as main categories.
Identifies a lack of clear distinction between interpretability and debugability in existing literature.
Categorizes post-hoc explanations into Group A (what the model learned) and Group B (why specific predictions are made), each with model-agnostic and model-specific subgroups.
papers.limitation: Lack of clear distinction between interpretability and debugability in existing methodologies.
future_direction: Constructing bug-free predictive models to potentially alleviate the need for interpretability.
Work towards an axiomatic treatment of interpretability.
papers.abstract: The ubiquity of machine learning based predictive models in modern society naturally leads people to ask how trustworthy those models are? In predictive modeling, it is quite common to induce a trade-off between accuracy and interpretability. For instance, doctors would like to know how effective some treatment will be for a patient or why the model suggested a particular medication for a patient exhibiting those symptoms? We acknowledge that the necessity for interpretability is a consequence of an incomplete formalisation of the problem, or more precisely of multiple meanings adhered to a particular concept. For certain problems, it is not enough to get the answer (what), the model also has to provide an explanation of how it came to that conclusion (why), because a correct prediction, only partially solves the original problem. In this article we extend existing categorisation of techniques to aid model interpretability and test this categorisation.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability.
