papers.core_contribution: Introduces LinBridge, a learnable framework based on Jacobian analysis that decomposes nonlinear neural encoding models into a linear inherent component and a sample-selective mapping bias, enabling interpretable analysis and revealing hierarchical nonlinearity in the visual cortex.
papers.conclusion: LinBridge provides a novel tool for interpreting nonlinear neural encoding models and offers evidence for the hierarchical distribution of nonlinearity in the visual cortex, bridging the interpretability and nonlinearity divide.
papers.key_findings:
The linear inherent component extracted by LinBridge accurately reflects the complex mappings of nonlinear neural encoding models, showing high correlation with the original model's predictions.
The sample-selective mapping bias elucidates the variability of nonlinearity across different levels of the visual processing hierarchy, with nonlinearity increasing from primary to tertiary visual cortex.
Nonlinear encoding models outperform linear models in predicting brain activity, activating more voxels and achieving higher R^2 values in the visual cortex.
LinBridge demonstrates stable extraction of the linear inherent component across different batch sizes, indicating robustness.
Beyond the visual cortex, other brain regions associated with higher cognitive processing (e.g., TPOJ, prefrontal areas) also exhibit nonlinearity, suggesting complex nonlinear mechanisms in higher-order cognition.
papers.limitation:
Validation of LinBridge is performed using a simple nonlinear encoding model; future work should validate with more advanced models.
Computation of the Jacobian matrix is resource-intensive for large datasets, suggesting a need for more efficient methods like low-rank matrix decomposition.
The study focuses on the visual cortex; applying LinBridge to other modalities (acoustic, linguistic, multimodal) is a future direction.
future_direction: Conduct further validation studies using more advanced nonlinear encoding models.
Incorporate low-rank matrix decomposition for efficient computation of mapping relationships in large datasets.
Apply LinBridge to neural encoding models in other modalities such as acoustic, linguistic, and multimodal information.
papers.abstract: Neural encoding of artificial neural networks (ANNs) links their computational representations to brain responses, offering insights into how the brain processes information. Current studies mostly use linear encoding models for clarity, even though brain responses are often nonlinear. This has sparked interest in developing nonlinear encoding models that are still interpretable. To address this problem, we propose LinBridge, a learnable and flexible framework based on Jacobian analysis for interpreting nonlinear encoding models. LinBridge posits that the nonlinear mapping between ANN representations and neural responses can be factorized into a linear inherent component that approximates the complex nonlinear relationship, and a mapping bias that captures sample-selective nonlinearity. The Jacobian matrix, which reflects output change rates relative to input, enables the analysis of sample-selective mapping in nonlinear models. LinBridge employs a self-supervised learning strategy to extract both the linear inherent component and nonlinear mapping biases from the Jacobian matrices of the test set, allowing it to adapt effectively to various nonlinear encoding models. We validate the LinBridge framework in the scenario of neural visual encoding, using computational visual representations from CLIP-ViT to predict brain activity recorded via functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Our experimental results demonstrate that: 1) the linear inherent component extracted by LinBridge accurately reflects the complex mappings of nonlinear neural encoding models; 2) the sample-selective mapping bias elucidates the variability of nonlinearity across different levels of the visual processing hierarchy. This study presents a novel tool for interpreting nonlinear neural encoding models and offers fresh evidence about hierarchical nonlinearity distribution in the visual cortex.

papers.title: From Human Explanation to Model Interpretability: A Framework Based on Weight of Evidence
papers.research_question: How can we design interpretability methods that are meaningful to humans, inspired by the study of human explanation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a human-centered framework for interpretability based on weight of evidence, generating explanations that are contrastive, modular, and parsimonious.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for interpretability based on weight of evidence, showing it can generate human-centered explanations that are usable and robust.
papers.key_findings:
The weight of evidence (WoE) can be adapted to high-dimensional, multi-class settings to generate human-centered explanations.
WoE explanations can be accurately estimated from finite samples and are robust to small input perturbations.
A user study with ML practitioners showed that WoE explanations are usable, though some struggled with concepts like prior class probabilities.
The framework adheres to design principles derived from human explanation literature: contrastive, exhaustive, modular, understandable, and parsimonious.
The method is compared to LIME and SHAP, showing competitive robustness on benchmark datasets.
papers.limitation:
The WoE requires access to conditional likelihoods, which may be difficult to estimate for complex data types like images.
The user study had a limited number of participants and focused on ML practitioners, which may not generalize to other user groups.
future_direction: Adapting modern density estimation methods for complex data types like images to widen applicability.
Conducting follow-up user studies to investigate design choices like class partitioning techniques.
Longitudinal field studies with participants using their own models and data.
papers.abstract: We take inspiration from the study of human explanation to inform the design and evaluation of interpretability methods in machine learning. First, we survey the literature on human explanation in philosophy, cognitive science, and the social sciences, and propose a list of design principles for machine-generated explanations that are meaningful to humans. Using the concept of weight of evidence from information theory, we develop a method for generating explanations that adhere to these principles. We show that this method can be adapted to handle high-dimensional, multi-class settings, yielding a flexible framework for generating explanations. We demonstrate that these explanations can be estimated accurately from finite samples and are robust to small perturbations of the inputs. We also evaluate our method through a qualitative user study with machine learning practitioners, where we observe that the resulting explanations are usable despite some participants struggling with background concepts like prior class probabilities. Finally, we conclude by surfacing design implications for interpretability tools in general.

papers.title: Understanding Gated Neurons in Transformers from Their Input-Output Functionality
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between what a neuron reads and what it writes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parameter-based method to classify gated neurons in transformers by input-output weight similarity, finding that enrichment neurons dominate early-middle layers while depletion neurons are more common in later layers.
papers.conclusion: The input-output perspective complements activation-dependent analyses and approaches that treat input and output separately, providing insights into how neurons manipulate concepts in the residual stream.
papers.key_findings:
Enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers across all 12 models studied, whereas later layers tend more towards depletion neurons.
A large proportion of neurons are input manipulators, with conditional enrichment being the most common class, especially in early-middle layers.
Many neurons exhibit double checking, where gate and input weight vectors are approximately orthogonal but intuitively represent the same concept.
The median cosine similarity between input and output weights is positive in early layers and negative in later layers, indicating a smooth transition in functionality.
Neurons rarely have prototypical weight configurations; instead, they often add novel but related information to the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method is parameter-based and therefore limited in scope; it is not designed to replace other neuron analysis methods.
Mathematical similarities of weights may not reflect semantic similarity; orthogonal vectors can represent similar concepts, and similar vectors can represent non-identical concepts.
Case studies of individual neurons may be cherry-picked, focusing on interpretable neurons in later layers, so interpretations may not generalize.
The paper provides only possible interpretations of observed phenomena, not definitive explanations.
future_direction: Extend the method to non-gated activation functions.
Study the evolution of input-output functionalities during model training.
Go beyond the analysis of single neurons to understand how neurons work together within and across classes.
papers.abstract: Interpretability researchers have attempted to understand MLP neurons of language models based on both the contexts in which they activate and their output weight vectors. They have paid little attention to a complementary aspect: the interactions between input and output. For example, when neurons detect a direction in the input, they might add much the same direction to the residual stream ("enrichment neurons") or reduce its presence ("depletion neurons"). We address this aspect by examining the cosine similarity between input and output weights of a neuron. We apply our method to 12 models and find that enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers whereas later layers tend more towards depletion. To explain this finding, we argue that enrichment neurons are largely responsible for enriching concept representations, one of the first steps of factual recall. Our input-output perspective is a complement to activation-dependent analyses and to approaches that treat input and output separately.

papers.title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Language Through a Prism: A Spectral Approach for Multiscale Language Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do deep models capture information at different linguistic scales (from subwords to documents), and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a spectral filtering framework and a prism layer to disentangle and control multiscale linguistic information in deep language representations, enabling scale-specific analysis and improved modeling of long-range dependencies.
papers.conclusion: Spectral techniques provide a principled and effective framework for uncovering and modeling multiscale phenomena in deep NLP models, with potential applications in interpretability and other domains.
papers.key_findings:
Spectral filters can separate scale-specific information in BERT's neuron activations, with high-pass filters best for word-level tasks and low-pass filters best for document-level tasks.
Training BERT with a prism layer, which forces neurons to specialize in different frequency bands, produces multiscale representations that improve performance on utterance- and document-level tasks while maintaining word-level performance.
The BERT + Prism model shows increased sensitivity to long-range context in masked language modeling, as evidenced by higher log probabilities for masked tokens without local context.
future_direction: Applying spectral tools for interpretability to understand knowledge and information processing at different scales.
Using the method to track topics over time or remove extraneous information in linguistic change research.
Extending the method to other domains with geometric structure, such as computer vision, time series, and reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Language exhibits structure at different scales, ranging from subwords to words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents. To what extent do deep models capture information at these scales, and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy? We approach this question by focusing on individual neurons, analyzing the behavior of their activations at different timescales. We show that signal processing provides a natural framework for separating structure across scales, enabling us to 1) disentangle scale-specific information in existing embeddings and 2) train models to learn more about particular scales. Concretely, we apply spectral filters to the activations of a neuron across an input, producing filtered embeddings that perform well on part of speech tagging (word-level), dialog speech acts classification (utterance-level), or topic classification (document-level), while performing poorly on the other tasks. We also present a prism layer for training models, which uses spectral filters to constrain different neurons to model structure at different scales. Our proposed BERT + Prism model can better predict masked tokens using long-range context and produces multiscale representations that perform better at utterance- and document-level tasks. Our methods are general and readily applicable to other domains besides language, such as images, audio, and video.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of\n Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the stacked layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interventional, input perturbation-based analysis method to show that Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, with larger contexts and more complex phrase boundaries becoming more salient in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process; structured input perturbations are a useful tool for analyzing deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing characteristic scale of context along layers.
Swapping two constituent phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrase spans of the same length, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, indicating sensitivity to phrase hierarchy.
Changes in attention weights partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance, with deeper layers showing more correlation.
The observed sensitivities are not due to simple co-occurrence statistics, as shown by controlling for PMI.
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features
Searching for the causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance
Exploring applications in network pruning studies
Extending the method as a hypothesis generator in neuroscience to understand compositional structure in neural populations
papers.abstract:
While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models
have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete
accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear
what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations,
nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In
this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of
interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from
pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive
neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of
probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several
kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a
sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the
original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random
permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a
representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which
do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase
structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break
apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure.
 Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build
sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that
hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our
results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of
analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can
serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for
interpreting complex black-box models.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: Interpretability in Parameter Space: Minimizing Mechanistic Description Length with Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we decompose neural network parameters into faithful, minimal, and simple mechanistic components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components that are faithful, minimal, and simple, optimizing for minimal description length.
papers.conclusion: APD offers a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, suggesting solutions to open problems like identifying minimal circuits in superposition and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition, though challenges remain for scaling.
papers.key_findings:
APD successfully recovers ground truth mechanisms in a toy model of superposition, decomposing the weight matrix into columns corresponding to individual features.
APD identifies parameter components representing individual functions in a toy model of compressed computation, where the model computes more nonlinear functions than it has neurons.
APD learns components that represent individual functions even when they span multiple layers in a toy model of cross-layer distributed representations.
APD's components are faithful to the original parameters, minimal in number per input, and simple in terms of rank.
papers.limitation:
High computational cost due to the need for multiple forward and backward passes.
Sensitivity to hyperparameters, such as the batch top-k value and loss coefficients.
Attributions are approximated using gradients, which may not perfectly capture causal importance.
future_direction: Improving computational cost
Improving robustness to hyperparameters
Improving attributions
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. Despite recent progress toward this goal, it remains unclear how best to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components. We introduce Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method that directly decomposes a neural network's parameters into components that (i) are faithful to the parameters of the original network, (ii) require a minimal number of components to process any input, and (iii) are maximally simple. Our approach thus optimizes for a minimal length description of the network's mechanisms. We demonstrate APD's effectiveness by successfully identifying ground truth mechanisms in multiple toy experimental settings: Recovering features from superposition; separating compressed computations; and identifying cross-layer distributed representations. While challenges remain to scaling APD to non-toy models, our results suggest solutions to several open problems in mechanistic interpretability, including identifying minimal circuits in superposition, offering a conceptual foundation for 'features', and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition.

papers.title: On the Mechanistic Interpretability of Neural Networks for Causality in Bio-statistics
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability techniques be transposed to bio-statistics, and how effective are they?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability tools can be leveraged to probe and validate internal representations learned by neural networks for causal inference, discover and visualize computational pathways for confounders and treatments, and compare learned mechanisms across model types.
papers.abstract: Interpretable insights from predictive models remain critical in bio-statistics, particularly when assessing causality, where classical statistical and machine learning methods often provide inherent clarity. While Neural Networks (NNs) offer powerful capabilities for modeling complex biological data, their traditional "black-box" nature presents challenges for validation and trust in high-stakes health applications. Recent advances in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aim to decipher the internal computations learned by these networks. This work investigates the application of MI techniques to NNs within the context of causal inference for bio-statistics. We demonstrate that MI tools can be leveraged to: (1) probe and validate the internal representations learned by NNs, such as those estimating nuisance functions in frameworks like Targeted Minimum Loss-based Estimation (TMLE); (2) discover and visualize the distinct computational pathways employed by the network to process different types of inputs, potentially revealing how confounders and treatments are handled; and (3) provide methodologies for comparing the learned mechanisms and extracted insights across statistical, machine learning, and NN models, fostering a deeper understanding of their respective strengths and weaknesses for causal bio-statistical analysis.

papers.title: Towards Tracing Knowledge in Language Models Back to the Training Data
papers.research_question: How can we identify which training examples taught a language model to generate a particular factual assertion?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the problem of fact tracing and presents the first quantitative benchmark (FTRACE) to evaluate training data attribution methods for tracing factual knowledge in language models back to specific training examples.
papers.conclusion: Significant headroom remains for improving training data attribution methods for fact tracing, with key challenges including gradient saturation and the importance of nuanced implementation details.
papers.key_findings:
Current TDA methods (gradient-based TRACIN and embedding-based EMBED) underperform a simple IR baseline (BM25) on the natural fact tracing benchmark (FTRACE-TREx).
On the controlled synthetic benchmark (FTRACE-SYNTH), TDA methods show better upper bounds, indicating potential when lexical overlap is reduced.
Optimizing TDA hyperparameters (e.g., layer selection, gradient normalization, using optimizer accumulators) significantly improves performance.
The embedding layer provides the most reliable attribution signal for both gradient and embedding-based methods.
Gradient saturation is a key challenge for TDA methods when facts are already known by the model.
papers.limitation:
Gradient saturation: when a model already knows a fact, gradients are near zero, making it difficult for TDA methods to attribute.
The natural benchmark (FTRACE-TREx) may have lexical overlap that favors surface-level IR methods like BM25.
future_direction: Improving TDA methods to overcome the gradient saturation problem.
Better handling of indirect proponents (facts inferred from other facts).
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) have been shown to memorize a great deal of factual knowledge contained in their training data. But when an LM generates an assertion, it is often difficult to determine where it learned this information and whether it is true. In this paper, we propose the problem of fact tracing: identifying which training examples taught an LM to generate a particular factual assertion. Prior work on training data attribution (TDA) may offer effective tools for identifying such examples, known as “proponents”. We present the first quantitative benchmark to evaluate this. We compare two popular families of TDA methods — gradient-based and embedding-based — and find that much headroom remains. For example, both methods have lower proponent-retrieval precision than an information retrieval baseline (BM25) that does not have access to the LM at all. We identify key challenges that may be necessary for further improvement such as overcoming the problem of gradient saturation, and also show how several nuanced implementation details of existing neural TDA methods can significantly improve overall fact tracing performance.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Assessing the Local Interpretability of Machine Learning Models
papers.research_question: What does it mean for a machine learning model to be interpretable by humans, and how can this be assessed? The paper focuses on two definitions: simulatability and 'what if' local explainability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes runtime operation count as a metric for local interpretability and shows through a user study that as operation count increases, human accuracy decreases, supporting the common intuition that decision trees and logistic regression are more interpretable than neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The work provides evidence for folk hypotheses about interpretability and that runtime operations metric gives insight into local interpretability, but further work is needed to generalize the metric and understand the causes of interpretability limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Decision trees and logistic regression are locally interpretable (simulatable and 'what if' explainable), while neural networks are not.
Decision trees are more locally interpretable than logistic regression and neural networks.
Logistic regression is more 'what if' locally explainable and locally interpretable than neural networks, but not more simulatable.
As the number of runtime operations increases, the time taken by users increases.
As the number of runtime operations increases, accuracy decreases for decision trees, but the trend is not clear for logistic regression and neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The domain-agnostic synthetic dataset may not capture interpretability within its target domain.
The definitions of local interpretability assessed (simulatability and 'what if' local explainability) are limited in their reach.
The user study setup may be limited in capturing the nuance of these definitions.
It is unclear if users' inability to locally interpret large neural networks is due to the number of operation counts or neural networks themselves, because other models with similar operation counts were not tested.
future_direction: Further work is needed to consider the extent to which the metric generalizes to other model types.
Further work is needed to verify if users' inability to locally interpret large neural networks was caused by the number of operation counts or neural networks themselves.
This work provides a starting point for designing user studies to validate notions of interpretability in machine learning.
papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of machine learning tools has led to calls for accountability via model interpretability. But what does it mean for a machine learning model to be interpretable by humans, and how can this be assessed? We focus on two definitions of interpretability that have been introduced in the machine learning literature: simulatability (a user's ability to run a model on a given input) and "what if" local explainability (a user's ability to correctly determine a model's prediction under local changes to the input, given knowledge of the model's original prediction). Through a user study with 1,000 participants, we test whether humans perform well on tasks that mimic the definitions of simulatability and "what if" local explainability on models that are typically considered locally interpretable. To track the relative interpretability of models, we employ a simple metric, the runtime operation count on the simulatability task. We find evidence that as the number of operations increases, participant accuracy on the local interpretability tasks decreases. In addition, this evidence is consistent with the common intuition that decision trees and logistic regression models are interpretable and are more interpretable than neural networks.

papers.title: Correlation of internal representations in feed-forward neural networks
papers.research_question: How do correlations between hidden node activities in feed-forward neural networks arise near saturation, and how can they be calculated for arbitrary decoder functions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows how to calculate correlations between hidden node activities in feed-forward neural networks near saturation, and provides explicit formulas for parity, AND, and committee machines.
papers.conclusion: The correlations between hidden nodes in feed-forward neural networks near saturation can be calculated and are determined by the decoder function, and these results are likely robust to replica symmetry breaking.
papers.key_findings:
For the parity-machine, all legal internal representations have equal probability, leading to zero correlations for n<K and cK=1.
For the AND-machine, correlations are dominated by the restrictive output case σ=+1, resulting in cn = 1/2 - n2^{-K}/K.
For the committee-machine, correlations are given by explicit formulas (13) and (14), with specific asymptotic behavior for large K.
The correlations near saturation are determined by the decoder function and the distribution of internal representations.
The results rely on replica symmetry but are likely robust to replica symmetry breaking.
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes replica symmetry, while replica symmetry breaking is known to be crucial for storage capacity calculations.
future_direction: Determine the storage capacity of an ensemble of uncoupled perceptrons with prescribed correlations.
papers.abstract:
Feed-forward multilayer neural networks implementing random input-output
mappings develop characteristic correlations between the activity of their
hidden nodes which are important for the understanding of the storage and
generalization performance of the network. It is shown how these correlations
can be calculated from the joint probability distribution of the aligning
fields at the hidden units for arbitrary decoder function between hidden layer
and output. Explicit results are given for the parity-, and-, and
committee-machines with arbitrary number of hidden nodes near saturation.

papers.title: Saturating Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: How does a saturation regularizer affect auto-encoders' ability to reconstruct inputs near and away from the data manifold?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a saturation regularizer for auto-encoders that encourages activations in saturated regions, limiting reconstruction of off-manifold inputs and enabling learning of diverse features depending on the activation function.
papers.conclusion: Introduces a general and conceptually simple latent state regularizer for auto-encoders that can learn a variety of feature sets depending on the activation function, with connections to existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The saturation regularizer explicitly limits the auto-encoder's ability to reconstruct inputs not near the data manifold.
SATAE-shrink is equivalent to a sparse auto-encoder with L1 penalty on activations.
SATAE-saturated-linear learns an identity basis on binary data but a more varied basis on natural image patches.
With increasing saturation penalty, basis elements in SATAE-shrink become less spatially localized, while in SATAE-SL they align with data to facilitate reconstruction.
Connections are established with Contractive and Sparse Auto-Encoders, showing SATAEs generalize sparse auto-encoders.
papers.limitation:
How to select or learn the width parameter λ of the nonlinearity is an open question.
How to methodically constrain the weights is an open question.
future_direction: Experimentally demonstrate that representations learned by SATAEs are useful for tasks like classification and denoising.
Address how to select or learn the width parameter λ of the nonlinearity.
Explore SATAEs with a wider class of non-linearities and architectures.
papers.abstract: We introduce a simple new regularizer for auto-encoders whose hidden-unit activation functions contain at least one zero-gradient (saturated) region. This regularizer explicitly encourages activations in the saturated region(s) of the corresponding activation function. We call these Saturating Auto-Encoders (SATAE). We show that the saturation regularizer explicitly limits the SATAE's ability to reconstruct inputs which are not near the data manifold. Furthermore, we show that a wide variety of features can be learned when different activation functions are used. Finally, connections are established with the Contractive and Sparse Auto-Encoders.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: Response Characterization for Auditing Cell Dynamics in Long Short-term Memory Networks
papers.research_question: How can we systematically interpret the hidden dynamics of LSTM networks at the cellular level using response characterization methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a response characterization method to interpret LSTM networks at the cellular level, enabling identification of important cells and analysis of their dynamical properties.
papers.conclusion: The proposed response characterization method effectively interprets LSTM dynamics at the cellular and network levels, providing a novel building block for LSTM interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Response metrics (settling time, delta response, sine amplitude, etc.) can identify fast and slow cells, and cells that contribute significantly to the network output.
The method generalizes across different sequential datasets (MNIST, stock prices, CO2 concentrations, protein sequences).
Ablation analysis validates that cells with high response metrics (delta response and sine amplitude) have a larger impact on network performance.
Network capacity analysis shows that as the number of LSTM cells increases, the amplitude of each cell's contribution decreases inversely.
The distribution of settling time is relatively constant across network capacities, indicating that the network learns time delays irrespective of size.
papers.limitation: The LSTM network's dynamic space is broad and cannot be fully captured by fundamental input sequences (step and sinusoid).
future_direction: Extend the approach to more data modalities.
Analyze the training phase of LSTMs to interpret the learning of converged dynamics.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel method to interpret recurrent neural networks (RNNs), particularly long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) at the cellular level. We propose a systematic pipeline for interpreting individual hidden state dynamics within the network using response characterization methods. The ranked contribution of individual cells to the network's output is computed by analyzing a set of interpretable metrics of their decoupled step and sinusoidal responses. As a result, our method is able to uniquely identify neurons with insightful dynamics, quantify relationships between dynamical properties and test accuracy through ablation analysis, and interpret the impact of network capacity on a network's dynamical distribution. Finally, we demonstrate the generalizability and scalability of our method by evaluating a series of different benchmark sequential datasets.

papers.title: A Framework for Interpretability in Machine Learning for Medical Imaging
papers.research_question: Why does the need for interpretability in machine learning for medical imaging (MLMI) arise? What are the underlying elements of interpretability in MLMI? How can we formalize these into a framework for interpretability in MLMI?
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes interpretability needs in medical imaging by identifying five core elements (localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability) and proposes a framework to guide practitioners in designing and evaluating interpretable MLMI methods.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes interpretability in medical imaging through a framework based on five core elements, aiming to guide method design, improve real-world usage, and inspire future research.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability in MLMI can be decomposed into five core elements: localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability.
A framework is proposed that connects real-world medical imaging tasks and objectives to these interpretability elements and existing methods.
The framework provides a step-by-step guide for practitioners to approach interpretability in MLMI, from defining the problem to selecting appropriate methods.
Interpretability methods should be chosen based on the specific real-world objectives (e.g., troubleshooting, fairness, trust) and the intended users (e.g., clinicians, researchers).
Pixel-level tasks (e.g., segmentation, registration) have inherent interpretability due to their localizable and visually recognizable outputs.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability might induce or contribute to human biases such as automation bias (too much trust) or algorithmic aversion (too much distrust).
Low-dimensional projections of high-dimensional internal representations (e.g., 2D heatmaps) can give users a false sense of understanding.
Interpretability is not always necessary and can potentially hinder model performance or introduce new biases.
future_direction: Developing interpretability methods that address multiple elements simultaneously.
Creating benchmarks and evaluation metrics specifically for interpretability methods in MLMI.
Studying the impact of interpretability on clinical decision-making and outcomes.
Exploring the role of interpretability in the regulatory approval of MLMI systems.
papers.abstract: Interpretability for machine learning models in medical imaging (MLMI) is an important direction of research. However, there is a general sense of murkiness in what interpretability means. Why does the need for interpretability in MLMI arise? What goals does one actually seek to address when interpretability is needed? To answer these questions, we identify a need to formalize the goals and elements of interpretability in MLMI. By reasoning about real-world tasks and goals common in both medical image analysis and its intersection with machine learning, we identify five core elements of interpretability: localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability. From this, we arrive at a framework for interpretability in MLMI, which serves as a step-by-step guide to approaching interpretability in this context. Overall, this paper formalizes interpretability needs in the context of medical imaging, and our applied perspective clarifies concrete MLMI-specific goals and considerations in order to guide method design and improve real-world usage. Our goal is to provide practical and didactic information for model designers and practitioners, inspire developers of models in the medical imaging field to reason more deeply about what interpretability is achieving, and suggest future directions of interpretability research.

papers.title: Looking Beyond The Top-1: Transformers Determine Top Tokens In Order
papers.research_question: What computation is the Transformer model performing after the saturation event (where the top-1 prediction becomes fixed)?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers determine their top-k output tokens in order of ranking via a discrete task-transition mechanism, a phenomenon intrinsic to the architecture that can be leveraged for improved early-exit strategies and language modeling.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Transformer layers after the top-1 saturation event work on determining lower-ranked tokens in order, proposes a task-transition mechanism underlying this, and shows practical benefits for efficiency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Top-k tokens in Transformers reach saturation (become fixed) sequentially in the order of their final ranking.
This ordered saturation occurs across text, vision, and speech modalities and in untrained models, suggesting it is architecture-inherent.
A simple classifier can predict the current 'task' (which token rank is being determined) from hidden layer embeddings.
Intervening by injecting activations from a saturation layer can causally trigger a transition to the next task.
A novel early-exit strategy based on task transition outperforms existing token-level confidence measures.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not determine which specific components in the Transformer architecture give rise to the ordered saturation phenomenon.
The work does not consider whether the data used was encountered during the models' training.
future_direction: Ablation studies to identify which Transformer components are responsible for the ordered saturation.
Investigating if other DNN architectures (e.g., RNNs) also determine top-k tokens in order.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Transformers is crucial for achieving more accurate and efficient predictions. In this work, we analyze the computation performed by Transformers in the layers after the top-1 prediction has become fixed, which has been previously referred to as the "saturation event". We expand the concept of saturation events for top-k tokens, demonstrating that similar saturation events occur across language, vision, and speech models. We find that these saturation events happen in order of the corresponding tokens' ranking, i.e., the model first decides on the top ranking token, then the second highest ranking token, and so on. This phenomenon seems intrinsic to the Transformer architecture, occurring across different architectural variants (decoder-only, encoder-only, and to a lesser extent full-Transformer), and even in untrained Transformers. We propose an underlying mechanism of task transition for this sequential saturation, where task k corresponds to predicting the k-th most probable token, and the saturation events are in fact discrete transitions between the tasks. In support of this we show that it is possible to predict the current task from hidden layer embedding. Furthermore, using an intervention method we demonstrate that we can cause the model to switch from one task to the next. Finally, leveraging our findings, we introduce a novel token-level early-exit strategy, which surpasses existing methods in balancing performance and efficiency.

papers.title: Image denoising with multi-layer perceptrons, part 2: training trade-offs and analysis of their mechanisms
papers.research_question: What trade-offs must be considered when training multi-layer perceptrons for image denoising, and how do these networks internally achieve denoising?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides detailed guidelines for training MLPs to achieve state-of-the-art image denoising and analyzes their inner workings, showing that denoising is achieved through saturation of the tanh activation function, leading to binary hidden representations.
papers.conclusion: MLPs can achieve excellent image denoising performance when trained with appropriate trade-offs, and their internal mechanisms can be understood through analysis of hidden unit activation patterns, revealing a denoising process based on saturation and binary codes.
papers.key_findings:
More training data and more hidden units per layer consistently improve performance.
There exists an ideal number of hidden layers; too many layers, especially in deep and narrow networks, can cause catastrophic performance degradation.
Fine-tuning with a lower learning rate after initial training reduces test error fluctuations and improves final performance.
Denoising in single-hidden-layer MLPs is achieved through saturation of the tanh layer, which attenuates noise while preserving features detected by highly active neurons.
The feature detectors (input weights) adapt to the noise type and strength; for example, larger input patches are learned for stronger noise.
papers.limitation:
Deep and narrow networks (with many hidden layers but few units per layer) are difficult to optimize and can suffer catastrophic degradation in performance.
Block-matching MLPs do not provide a clear advantage at very low or very high noise levels, and their performance can deteriorate compared to plain MLPs at high noise levels.
future_direction: Applying similar training guidelines and analysis to other image processing tasks like super-resolution, deconvolution, and demosaicking.
Exploring the benefits of binary representations compared to sparse representations in deep networks.
papers.abstract: Image denoising can be described as the problem of mapping from a noisy image to a noise-free image. In another paper, we show that multi-layer perceptrons can achieve outstanding image denoising performance for various types of noise (additive white Gaussian noise, mixed Poisson-Gaussian noise, JPEG artifacts, salt-and-pepper noise and noise resembling stripes). In this work we discuss in detail which trade-offs have to be considered during the training procedure. We will show how to achieve good results and which pitfalls to avoid. By analysing the activation patterns of the hidden units we are able to make observations regarding the functioning principle of multi-layer perceptrons trained for image denoising.

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: Analyzing Feed-Forward Blocks in Transformers through the Lens of Attention Maps
papers.research_question: How do feed-forward blocks in transformers modify input contextualization, and how do their effects interact with surrounding components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes feed-forward blocks in transformers and shows that they modify input contextualization to emphasize specific linguistic compositions, and that their effects are often canceled by surrounding residual and normalization layers, suggesting redundancy.
papers.conclusion: FF blocks in transformers modify input contextualization to emphasize linguistic compositions, but their effects are often canceled by surrounding components, suggesting redundancy in the transformer's internal processing.
papers.key_findings:
FF networks modify input contextualization, with larger changes in specific layers (e.g., middle to late layers in BERT, early layers in GPT-2).
FF amplifies specific types of linguistic compositions, such as subwords-to-word and words-to-multi-word-expression constructions.
The effects of FF are often canceled by subsequent residual and normalization layers, indicating redundancy in the transformer layer.
The cancellation is due to the large norm of the residual bypass vector and the shrinking of outlier dimensions by layer normalization.
The contextualization changes are not simply explained by word co-occurrence (low correlation with PMI).
papers.limitation: The method is computationally costly for large models and long inputs, making it challenging to apply to billion-scale LLMs.
future_direction: Lightening the computational cost of the method.
Experimenting with other datasets and models.
Investigating the cause of differences between BERT and GPT-2 in FF effects.
papers.abstract: Transformers are ubiquitous in wide tasks. Interpreting their internals is a pivotal goal. Nevertheless, their particular components, feed-forward (FF) blocks, have typically been less analyzed despite their substantial parameter amounts. We analyze the input contextualization effects of FF blocks by rendering them in the attention maps as a human-friendly visualization scheme. Our experiments with both masked- and causal-language models reveal that FF networks modify the input contextualization to emphasize specific types of linguistic compositions. In addition, FF and its surrounding components tend to cancel out each other's effects, suggesting potential redundancy in the processing of the Transformer layer.

papers.title: Response Characterization for Auditing Cell Dynamics in Long Short-term\n Memory Networks
papers.research_question: How can we systematically interpret the hidden dynamics of long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) at the cellular level using response characterization methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a response characterization method to interpret LSTM networks at the cellular level, enabling identification of important neurons and dynamics, validated by ablation analysis.
papers.conclusion: The proposed response characterization method provides a novel building block for interpreting LSTM networks, demonstrating that practical sub-regions of dynamics are reachable by response metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Response metrics (settling time, delta response, sine amplitude, etc.) can predict insightful dynamics for individual LSTM cells.
The method generalizes across different sequential datasets.
Response metrics predict significant contributing cells to the network's decision, as validated by ablation analysis.
Network capacity analysis shows that as network size increases, the amplitude of each cell's contribution decreases proportionally to 1/N.
The distribution of settling time is relatively constant across network capacity.
papers.limitation: The LSTM network's dynamic space is broad and cannot be fully captured by fundamental input sequences.
future_direction: Extend the approach to even more data modalities.
Analyze the training phase of LSTMs to interpret the learning of the converged dynamics.
papers.abstract:
In this paper, we introduce a novel method to interpret recurrent neural
networks (RNNs), particularly long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) at the
cellular level. We propose a systematic pipeline for interpreting individual
hidden state dynamics within the network using response characterization
methods. The ranked contribution of individual cells to the network's output is
computed by analyzing a set of interpretable metrics of their decoupled step
and sinusoidal responses. As a result, our method is able to uniquely identify
neurons with insightful dynamics, quantify relationships between dynamical
properties and test accuracy through ablation analysis, and interpret the
impact of network capacity on a network's dynamical distribution. Finally, we
demonstrate generalizability and scalability of our method by evaluating a
series of different benchmark sequential datasets.

papers.title: From Tokens to Words: On the Inner Lexicon of LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs encode words internally from sub-word tokens, and if so, how.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally detokenize sub-word tokens into whole-word representations in early to middle layers via an inner lexicon, enabling vocabulary expansion without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The work unravels the word detokenization process in LLMs, showing it occurs in early to middle layers and enables practical applications for optimizing tokenization and inference costs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can distinguish words from nonwords, with the distinction emerging in early to middle layers.
The last token of a word (even if split) can be decoded as the full word, indicating an inner lexicon.
FFN layers are crucial for retrieving full-word representations from the inner lexicon.
Attention patterns show early layers aggregate sub-word tokens, then later layers ignore them as the full word representation forms.
The inner lexicon can be used to expand the model's vocabulary without fine-tuning, reducing token count and maintaining performance.
papers.limitation:
22.6% of multi-token words are never successfully decoded, indicating the inner lexicon does not cover all words.
Vocabulary expansion success rate is lower for morphologically rich languages like Arabic (16%).
papers.abstract: Natural language is composed of words, but modern large language models (LLMs) process sub-words as input. A natural question raised by this discrepancy is whether LLMs encode words internally, and if so how.
